text.title: Cognitive Walkthrough: Basics Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for a single-pass cognitive walkthrough: the four questions asked per step, the frozen action sequence, the first-use-only scope of any claim, failure stories instead of verdicts, and the severity scale a method with no users is allowed to use.

rule.statement: Every entry in `step_evaluations` MUST answer all four questions for its step, each with yes/no plus a reason: Q1 will the user try to achieve the right effect? Q2 will the user notice that the correct action is available? Q3 will the user associate the correct action with the effect they want? Q4 after the action, will the user see that progress is being made toward the goal? A step with 1-3 answers is incomplete, not a shortened form.

rationale.source: Wharton, Rieman, Lewis & Polson, "The Cognitive Walkthrough Method: A Practitioner's Guide" (in Nielsen & Mack, Usability Inspection Methods, 1994)

rule.rationale: The four questions map to four distinct breakdowns — wrong goal, invisible control, mislabelled control, absent feedback. Dropping one silently declares that class of failure impossible: skip Q4 and every action that succeeds without visible confirmation passes the inspection.

rule.statement: `correct_steps` MUST be an ordered list of atomic interface actions (one click, one field entry, one submit) with the interface state named after each, and it MUST be written down and closed before the first question is asked. Discovering a better path mid-walkthrough is logged as an issue, not substituted into the sequence.

rationale.source: Polson, Lewis, Rieman & Wharton, "Cognitive walkthroughs: a method for theory-based evaluation of user interfaces" (IJMMS, 1992)

rule.rationale: A walkthrough simulates one exploratory path. Swapping the path when it starts failing removes the failing steps from the record, so the session ends with a clean report of a route no first-time user would have taken.

rule.statement: `persona` MUST state what the simulated user already knows before touching the interface: domain vocabulary they use, comparable products they have used, and what they do NOT know. "New user" alone is rejected.

rationale.source: Polson & Lewis, CE+ theory of exploratory learning (Human-Computer Interaction, 1990)

rule.rationale: Q3 is a label-matching judgement — the user picks the control whose wording overlaps their goal wording. Without the user's assumed vocabulary written down, evaluators substitute their own, and every product-internal term ("Entities", "Workspaces") passes Q3 by default.

rule.statement: Each "no" answer MUST record a failure story: what the user would believe at that moment and what they would do instead (which wrong control, which back-out, which abandonment). A "no" with no story is not a finding and does not enter `issues`.

rationale.source: Wharton et al., Practitioner's Guide — credible success/failure story requirement

rule.rationale: The fix is derivable from the wrong belief, not from the verdict. "No — the label is unclear" supports no design change; "they will read Archive as delete and stop" names both the label and the reassurance that is missing.

rule.statement: Every step MUST be evaluated on the assumption that all preceding steps succeeded, and any issue found at step N MUST be marked as making steps N+1..end conditional. Findings on steps after a blocking failure MUST NOT be reported as independently confirmed.

rationale.source: Wharton et al., Practitioner's Guide — sequential walkthrough procedure

rule.rationale: The method walks a single chain of states. A user blocked at step 3 never reaches step 7, so the step-7 evaluation describes a state they cannot enter; treating those findings as equal-weight sends fix effort to screens nobody currently sees.

rule.statement: `issues[].severity` MUST use a blocking-based scale — blocker (user cannot proceed) / detour (user recovers via a wrong branch) / hesitation (user proceeds but uncertain) — and MUST NOT use frequency, impact-times-frequency, or "% of users affected".

rationale.source: Nielsen severity rating (frequency x impact x persistence) contrasted with inspection-without-users

rule.rationale: Frequency-weighted severity needs observed users; a cognitive walkthrough has none, so any percentage in the report is a fabricated number that will later be quoted as measurement. Blocking is the only dimension the method actually observes.

rule.statement: Skip when (a) the question is efficiency, error rate, satisfaction or task time rather than first-use learnability — route to moderated usability testing; (b) all real users are trained or repeat users, so no first-encounter exists; (c) the task is not goal-directed and linear (open browsing, exploratory dashboards) and no single correct sequence can be written; (d) no artefact shows the interface state after each action — a labelled wireframe is the minimum, a feature list is not.

rationale.source: Methodology preconditions in Wharton et al., Practitioner's Guide

rule.rationale: Without a definable correct sequence and a per-state interface, Q2 and Q4 have nothing to inspect; the session degenerates into a design critique whose output looks like walkthrough findings but rests on no simulated user.
